title: Is my AI game dev workflow a bad idea?
author: Eshinio
selftext:
Can I ask what you guys general workflow is when using AI to help create a game (in Unity)? For myself, I currently have this setup and I wanted to hear if it makes sense or it's a stupid approach:

1. Using desktop/Claude.ai chat as my "advisor" and prompt maker for the game. The entire game is planned out in phases and the chat will generate prompt001, 002, 003, etc. as .md files, which I then copy into a "Prompt" folder in my Unity project.
2. Within Unity, I launch Claude Code in terminal from the project root, enabled with various skills and connected with MCP. I then ask it to read the promptxxx.md file and execute everything in there. It performs the coding as instructed.
3. Afterwards, I report back to desktop/claude.ai with the results, either it works and we continue to next prompt - or there is a problem, where it will then create a prompt\_fix.md file, which I then ask Claude Code to run.

My question is, is it better to have the ENTIRE process through the terminal Claude Code, which is connected to the MCP and is that how you guys are doing it? Or you "split" the work like in my case?

comments.author: Ohgood9002
comments.body:
Claude for design and core systems. Codex for big fixes and iterateing on top of/fixing what claude does.

Claude designs the car, codex is the mechanic. This is the workflow many of us are using. The $20 claude sub + $20 codex sub.

Claude can do it all, but its gonna eat up usage way faster. Using codex alongside claude has ended up being more budget friendly for a lot of us. 

Really all you have to do is create a "implementation" markdown file. This is where claude and codex record what they have implemented into the project so the two agents can "talk" to each other

replies.author: Embarrassed_Split236
replies.body: Implementation file is smart, is this a separate doc per system or one big file that has info and public functions for every script?

replies.body: U guys are ages ahead of me … loved it

replies.author: Ohgood9002
replies.body:
I have mine set to one big file. All my documentation (systems, design specs etc) has also been uploaded as .MD files as well. That way the agents are using the correct project terminology when referencing uodates they have made to the project, so when they update the implementation log the correct 
.md files are updated too, like system implementation plans or project roadmaps.

I still have the AI agents manually audit the project and align documentation every so often to catch fringe cases

replies.author: timbo2m
replies.body: Separate docs with an index, keep LLM context small and avoid compaction at all costs.

I have also thought of adding early outs in the docs likes in traditional programming in hopes to cut down on token usage and context window management.

comments.author: HealthyWest6482
comments.body:
1. is useful. Spitballing with browser agent is helpful because inline CC/Codex these boys just wanna work like crackheads - so ideation/concepts is almost always more organic outside of the agentic workflow. If I'm looking for a heavy refactor I'll consult the context with the browser side agent and then ask the inline coder to sanity check what the browser agent suggests against the codebase. 

3. I'm not sure how unity MCP works but I believe both GPT and Claude browser has functionality where you can link your repo/source files to the browser agent to check how things land in the codebase itself.

Is it better to have the entire process through CC? I think it doesn't hurt sometimes - what you're dealing with mostly is scope. CC has a context window, feeding the context window helps with successful results in so that treating CC strictly as an executor will depend on whether or not claude web is grounded in its prompt suggestions.

I regularly will build context with inline coders before relative execution but will use the browser agent to brainstorm large changes before approaching inline. For example if I want to change how a specific feature works, to build context I'll ask "How does x feature currently work? Can we trace it" -> agent finds the feature, traces it back to the root and builds understanding of it -> "Based off how the feature works, is it safe and effective to have it 'xyz'?"

Wording is kinda key in two ways here. Keeping the concept neutral and not leaning into desired outcome prevents it from reinforcing a terrible idea. You might ask "Let's fit this square into a circle slot" and Claude Code will be like yeah let's do it motherfucker, great idea. Keeping it in the form of a question also allows the agent to build context (directed to search for grounding) instead of leaning into assumptions to hastily satisfy a broad demand, although I notice that Opus loves to assume regardless.

comments.author: kalvinbastello
comments.body:
I started with copilot advising which had good design ideas, before getting vsc and using gpt 5 mini, which sometimes was frustrating. Since 5.3 codex have relied more and more for it to donstuff and does well. Still rely on copilot for most advising and do math/tables/simple data tracking.

I don't know what I'm doing, so take as you will.

comments.author: verbalbacklash
comments.body: I agree with ohgood9002, I used Claude to help me write and prototype all the plot and game play logic out side of the engine then use that prototype to build with codex inside. That way I knew I sound game logic loops and ending all worked out and can use it as a direct fact check reference for codex to compare game state at any given time. It also help me to cut fat before I drug myself into so much scope creep that I would never even get to building.

comments.author: Former_Produce1721
comments.body: I use codex for it all wih great results

comments.author: stellarton
comments.body:
The workflow is not stupid, but I’d add one guardrail: never let a prompt file be “the truth” by itself.

For Unity especially, keep a small human-owned dev log next to those prompts. After each AI coding pass, write what actually changed, what broke, what you tested in Play Mode, and what decision you do not want reversed later. Otherwise prompt001, prompt002, prompt003 slowly turn into a mythology that may not match the project anymore.

I’d also keep each implementation prompt painfully small. One system, one scene, one acceptance test. Game projects get weird fast when the AI is allowed to touch architecture, UI, and balance in the same pass.
